title: The Slate
passages:
The Marrow lay bow-to a sea that kept arriving, and everything on her deck that wasn't lashed was trying to leave. Wren knelt in the lee of the wheelhouse with her back to the wind, the reader in her lap — a scuffed orange box the size of a bread loaf, a full-face mask coiled off one side of it. Her forearm had stopped bleeding into her sleeve and started bleeding onto the case. She wiped it on her trousers without looking.

"Sit down, Captain."

Sol sat, on the winch drum, hands in her lap like a woman at a bus stop. "You going to tell me what the box does, or do I guess?"

"It reads slates." Wren turned her collar down. Set in the skin at the collarbone, in a bed of yellow resin the size of a playing card, was the slate: the glass that takes down everything a diver sees and hears for as long as she stays under. "Yours is furred over. Hold still, this is the part you complain about."

She got a thumbnail under the resin and peeled it back in one curl, clipped the lead, and felt the reader wake up against her knees.

"It builds what's on there into something your head will take. You watch it through the mask, you get your hours back. The ones it caught. Not the ones it didn't — the slate's the only witness aboard and it's a bad one, it only writes down what was in front of your face."

"And if it wasn't in front of my face?"

"Then far as the boat's concerned it didn't happen."

Teo was rasping behind her. Not crying. Just the long wet haul of a boy whose scrubber — the cartridge that eats the carbon out of a breath — had an hour left in it, generous. Nia had him inside her coat and her chin came up like a dog's when Wren glanced back.

Wren checked the glass in its brass case on the bulkhead. The needle had walked off the bottom of the weather she'd read at dawn. "Factor's barge left the mole forty minutes back," she said. "Heard him tell somebody he was coming to collect."

"Collect what," Sol said. "Hold's empty."

"No," Wren agreed. "It is."

Dey was coiling drum line, slow and cheerful, stacking loops on his forearm like a man with all night and nothing planned. Twelve thousand gone out of the year he had left to buy, and he looked rested about it.

While the build spun up, Wren pulled Dey's log. She kept her voice flat, the way she did for the crew, and said the true thing out loud for once. "Your splice held. Cut went in at 06:12, verified, checksum clean. I took the name out of your build and it stayed out."

"Good," Dey said, agreeable.

"So you didn't keep it because I missed it. You kept it because you kept it."

"I don't know what I kept," Dey said. "It's nice not knowing."

Sol watched Wren's hands on the box. "So you're the one who tells people who they are."

"I hand people their own hours. What they do with them is their business."

"That isn't what I asked."

"No," Wren said. "It isn't."

The box chirped and text started crawling up its little screen, the transcript it wrote as it worked, naming every voice it knew. In the wheelhouse the radio muttered on the backup channel, open, unanswered, the way it had been open since noon.

"Salas," Dey said, easy, to nobody, the way a man reads a label off a tin.

Wren looked at the screen.

SALAS. 00:00:04.

Four seconds into her captain's day. Timestamped before Sol went over the side, before the drone, before the choice, before anyone aboard the Marrow had said that name out loud.

Wren looked at the timestamp the way you look at a dog that has followed you home. Then she did what she always did with a name she hadn't put on a slate. Nothing.

*Cheaper not to know*, she told the back of her neck. She woke her captain instead.

"Wren Achebe. Mercy General. You went down the line after Okafor."

The slate under her thumbnail ticked once, the way it did when it took a name. Wren sat very still. On the box the transcript scrolled up past SALAS, and now ACHEBE sat under it, fresh as paint. She had woken Sol maybe two hundred times, a hand on her shoulder, the same four words. The slate had heard every one. It had never once written her down.

She started the splice. The build ran twenty-six minutes of water into forty seconds of glass, and the box played it through the lens.

Dey came to watch, still cheerful, with a loop of drum line over his arm. Nia did not move, and did not look away. The lens filled with grey.

They went down the line together, Sol's hands and Dey's heels. At the ward, Dey let go of the tether. Through Sol's eyes he was a small warm shape on the bottom, sitting against the case with his mask fogged. Then a girl stood over him with a spring cell in one fist, cranking, her mouth going the whole time. The mask carried it.

*You're not him.*

Then the radio in Sol's mask, crisp as a bell: the Factor, asking for a count.

The lens tipped. The drone hung in the doorway, its lamp on the case, the case's lid furred with a year of frost. And then Sol's hands. A glove closed on the drone's housing and folded it, once, the way you'd fold a letter you'd decided not to send.

Nia's mouth opened and shut.

Wren knew what the needle had done all through that hour. She'd watched it do it. Her own voice came out of the mask speaker, small and far away, telling Sol there was ninety bar on her back and the drum had one pull in it, and to come up. It sounded like somebody's mother.

*"Cargo's people,"* said the woman on the glass, flat as a man reading a number off a meter. *"No count. Send the kid up, and the children. All the air you've got. I'll walk up slow."*

The hands on the glass let go of the line. The last of the powered drum whined away overhead, hauling three people toward a boat it would never see again. The lens watched them go. It did not pan, because eyes can't. It only held, the way a person holds still in the dark when the last of something leaves the room.

Then the gauge. Ninety. Alone. Sol's own breath in her own mask, slow as a clock.

Nobody said anything. Dey had stopped coiling.

At the very tail a new voice bled in under Sol's breathing, worn thin by four hundred meters of open water and whatever else was in the way, a man's, patient.

*Tell the kid to keep going down. Tell him Salas said so.*

The build hit the end and the lens went clear. Sol sat with her hands in her lap and looked at them, turning them over, a thumb working at a callus.

Then the radio in the wheelhouse cleared its throat. The backup channel. Still open. Still answered by nobody.

*"Wren."*

Not a call. A word laid down flat, the way the woman on the glass had said *people.*

Dey looked at the wheelhouse, then at Wren, and smiled like a man watching weather come in over a friend's house.

The chain groaned through the hawsepipe. The Marrow's bow lifted, swung, and the anchor line — scope, the rope they'd paid out to hold the boat against the tower — went slack, then tight with a crack that made the deck planks sing. They were dragging. The drowned tower loomed closer, its black windows empty, concrete ribs showing above the swell.

"Scope!" Wren shouted over the wind. She shoved the reader inside her coat, against her ribs, where the build was loaded and her thumb rested on the edit key.

Nia had Teo against her chest, one arm locked around him, but the boat was heeling, starboard rail going under the chop. Teo's feet scrabbled on the wet deck. He slid toward the rail, small and quiet, his breath a wet whistle behind the mask.

"Grab him!" Wren yelled.

Nia caught Teo by the coat, hauled him back against her own body. Her knuckles were white on the rail. "You're going to swamp us," she said.

"We're already swimming," Wren said. "Hand me the line."

She took the anchor rode hand over hand, the rope burning her palms, coiling and uncoiling around her fists. Nia took the other side of the bitt, and they hauled against the drift. Wind came across the deck in sheets, salt in Wren's teeth. She planted her boots against the bitt and leaned back, using her weight. Nia grunted beside her, Teo tucked under her chin.

The Marrow swung slower, stern to the sea now, the tower's shadow falling across the deck. Dey stood at the winch drum, drum line still coiled on his forearm, watching them with that loose, cheerful blankness of a man who had forgotten why the ocean was dangerous.

"Dey," Wren said. "Grab a turn."

"I don't remember how," Dey said. He smiled.

Wren hauled another armful, her shoulders burning, the rope tight in her gloves. The reader thumped against her side, the mask coiled tight. If it went over the scuppers — the drain holes in the rail that let seawater run off — it was gone, and Sol's hours with it. She shifted it under her arm, her thumb still on the edit key, the splice waiting, the kind version, the lie she'd tell again if she had to. Sol sat on the drum behind her, hands in her lap, watching nothing.

The chain bit. The Marrow stopped swinging. For a moment she held her breath.

Then she saw it.

The barge light sat low and clear on the water, closing, coming straight for them through the storm.

Teo's whistle stopped.

Not softened — stopped, in the middle of a breath, and his chest sat there without finishing it.

Nia's head came up off her brother. "Fix it." Not a question. "Do something, topside."

"I'm doing it." Wren was already down in the runoff on her knees with her hand on Dey's rebreather, the rig of hoses and canisters that takes a diver's own breath and loops it back instead of throwing it away. There on the loop's spine sat the cartridge — a sealed canister packed with soda lime, the grey granules that pull the carbon out of a spent breath so the next one is worth something.

She got the old cartridge out of Teo's collar. It came free warm and soft at the core, spent, its soda lime gone to chalk that couldn't hold another lungful. She spun the seal off Dey's fresh one and cranked it into the boy's mask until it clicked. The granules were cold against her thumb.

"Hold him level," she said. "Count with me. One. Two."

Nia held her brother with both arms and her chin locked, glaring the whole time like this was being done to her. Maybe it was.

On three Teo's chest caught. On four he pulled a breath all the way down, ugly and wet, and then another behind it, and his eyes came open.

"There," Wren said. "He's back."

"How long," Nia said.

"Hours." Wren didn't sweeten it. "A fresh cell buys him hours. Not days. I want that out of my mouth before it's out of the water."

Nia looked at her, and whatever moved behind the glare got shoved back down where she kept it. "You could have left the case. Us. All of it, down there in the dark."

"I know," Wren said.

Dey had drifted over, hands empty, that agreeable slack on his face. He looked at his own rig, the bare collar where the cartridge used to sit, and shrugged like a man who'd handed somebody a light.

"Take it," he said. "I'm good going down."

"You'll want that back on you before the next line," Wren said.

"I don't know what I'll want," Dey said, and it seemed to please him.

Wren's arm was still open where the anchor line had got it, and the reader sat under her coat against her ribs with the splice loaded and her thumb on the edit key. Soda lime for the boy — that was one bargain. The other was still waiting to be struck.

Past the stern the barge light had quit pretending. It sat low and yellow on the black water, bigger than it had been a minute back, no other lights on it, a man in a boat who had already decided how the night would go.

Wren turned around.

Sol had left the winch drum. She stood a body-length off, hands loose at her sides, watching Wren the way Teo had watched the ceiling a minute ago — breath held, waiting to be told what she'd just done.

Sol was still waiting to be told what she'd done. Wren meant to tell her something.

She drew the reader out from under her coat and set it on her knees, in the lee of her own body where the wind couldn't reach the screen. "You did a hard thing today," she said. "I can make it lighter to carry."

She walked the timeline back with her thumb, the way she'd walked it a hundred times — down through grey water to the ward, past the drone folded in a glove, back to her own voice coming small out of the mask: *ninety bar, one pull, come up.* She stopped where Sol's hands let go of the line.

Here. This was the cut. Everything past it the woman had spent — the year, the berths, the whole reason the Marrow sat six kilometers out in a rising sea — spent on two children she'd known an hour. Take this stretch out and Sol kept the warm part: she pulled three people out of the dark. Take it out and she never learned the price of the pulling.

Wren set the in-point at the refusal. Set the out at the gauge reading ninety and a woman breathing alone. Her thumb came down on the edit key, the one worn smooth, the one that had never once failed her.

"What are you doing."

Nia. She'd crossed the deck quiet with Teo on her shoulder, the fresh cartridge hissing at his collar. She was watching Wren's hands. Watching the thumb.

"My job," Wren said.

"Your job is cutting her." Low, flat, pitched under the wind so it wouldn't carry. "That's what the box does. I'm not stupid. You take a piece out and she keeps the rest and never knows it's gone. That's the trick. That's the whole trick."

Wren didn't answer, which was an answer.

"She went down past where people come back from." Nia's chin was up, the dog's chin, and her eyes were wet and furious and not spilling. "She looked at your money and she looked at us and she picked us. Said it out loud, on the glass. I heard her say *people.*" A breath. "She chose us. Say it. Say it to her face before you cut her tongue out of her own mouth."

"I don't remember," Dey offered from the drum, cheerful, to no one. "But it sounds like the truth. People like that. I think."

Past the stern the barge light had stopped pretending to be far off. It sat low and yellow and coming.

Wren looked at her captain.

Sol hadn't moved. Hands loose at her sides, that callus working under her thumb, and behind her eyes nothing at all but the wanting to be told. She was looking at the reader in Wren's lap.

"Who did I save, Wren?"

She asked it the way you ask a doctor. And she put out her hand — not for the box. For the mask coiled off the side of it, the thing that would set her own hours back into her head. Palm up. The way you take a thing from somebody you trust to tell you true.

Wren's thumb sat on the key.
